- Model consistently underestimates true prices, especially in the first 10–15 days of the forecast horizon.
- Forecasts show a gradual upward trend that fails to capture sharp, sudden spikes in true values (e.g., 70→80+).
- After a spike, model overestimates and then slowly decays — suggesting it doesn’t adjust quickly enough to sharp reversals.
- Model exhibits mean reversion bias: it tends to forecast toward a “middle” value after a spike, but true values often overshoot or undershoot more aggressively.
- Forecasts lag behind true values by 1–3 days in the early part of the horizon, especially when true values are rising sharply.
- Model is overly conservative in the early days of the forecast, underestimating volatility and upward momentum.
- When true values are below 70, model tends to overcorrect upward — forecasting higher than actual, then slowly drifting down.
- Model fails to capture the “tail” of the distribution — especially in the last 5–7 days of the forecast, where true values often dip sharply or show erratic behavior.
- Forecasts are smoother than true values — suggesting model lacks sensitivity to short-term volatility or sudden policy/seasonal shifts.
- Model tends to overfit recent trends, especially when recent history is trending upward — leading to overestimation of future prices.
